transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-30
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 45m
Attendees: Aisha Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood CSM), Evan Martinez (RiverMark), Sofia Ruiz (RiverMark), Daniel Kim (RiverMark)

Summary:
Quick sync on POC latency numbers; focus on TTFT (time-to-first-token), streaming vs non-streaming behaviour, sequence length impacts, and kernel choices/quantization tradeoffs. Agree to run targeted microbenchmarks and share CSVs; plan follow-up deep-dive.

Topics: TTFT, streaming, seq_len, kernel selection (triton/cutlass/custom), KV cache, batching, dedicated vs hosted latency SLOs

Transcript:
[00:00] Aisha: hey everyone, thanks for hopping on, quick intro — i'm aisha from redwood, liam our se will go through the numbers, priya on CSM.
[00:17] Evan: thanks, yeah we'll just jump in, we had the latest run from liam yesterday, noticed some spikes on the first token for longer prompts.
[00:31] Liam: yeah great, so you can see in the spreadsheet i dropped (link: https://redwood.app/benchmarks/rivermark) we ran base streaming and non-streaming on ded-4xA100 and hosted g4-family for parity. TTFT on ded averaged ~38ms for short seqs but for seq_len 1024 it pulled to ~95-120ms on some runs.
[01:05] Daniel: wait so 95 to 120ms is first token? that's higher than we expected for ded, suspicious. are you including compilation / kernel warmup?
[01:18] Liam: good call — these runs were cold for the kernel path; the first run included JIT-ish kernel selection and the model compilation step in our runtime. we saw a 10-30ms penalty on the very first request when kernels weren't cached. after a couple requests it's down to 40-60ms.
[01:40] Sofia: that matches our prod pattern, we have occasional cold starts, want to understand options — can we precompile or pin kernels?
[01:49] Liam: yes, two levers: 1) pre-warm (keep a tiny pool of warm workers), 2) snapshot compiled kernels in the dedicated deployment so the first request doesn't recompile. for hosted we do automatic caching but for private/dedicated we can bake artifacts during deploy.
[02:10] Evan: and streaming helps TTFT right? we thought streaming would get first token out faster.
[02:18] Liam: it usually does, but streaming introduces overhead when sequence lengths vary. if your prompts are long and you stream at sub-token granularity it can add micro-scheduling overhead. our numbers: for seq_len 256 streaming TTFT ~28ms, non-streaming ~35ms. for seq_len 1024 streaming was ~80ms vs non-streaming ~95ms — so streaming still wins but margin compresses.
[02:50] Aisha: could some of that be kv-cache or batching behavior?
[02:54] Liam: yeah the KV cache warm path matters. if you're pinning many similar contexts we hit the KV cache fast which reduces per-token time, but the first token still has to fetch and map KV so initial latency varies. Also batching policy — we saw a large batch when two concurrent requests landed which increased TTFT on the queued request.
[03:18] Daniel: what about quantization? we're looking at int8 to save cost, but worried about latency regressions.
[03:26] Liam: quantization helps throughput and can reduce tail latency on some kernels, but it also changes kernel choices. For instance, int8 path on our runtime uses a different GEMM kernel (cutlass-quant) which has different perf characteristics; sometimes single- token latency is slightly higher but tokens/sec is much better. it's a tradeoff.
[03:50] Sofia: hmm ok, do you have recommendations for our low-latency config? we need P95 < 200ms first-token, ideally 100ms.
[03:59] Liam: for P95 100ms at your target QPS (you told us earlier 60 rps peak), dedicated 4xA100 provisioned with pinning + pre-warm workers + streaming + seq_len capped at 512 for most service flows will get you there. For longer flows (1024+) we can do ded plus a small batching window and tune kernel selection to prefer fast float16 kernels (cutlass-fp16) — that keeps TTFT lower.
[04:35] Evan: you mentioned kernel selection — triton vs cutlass, what do you recommend?
[04:40] Liam: we auto-select, but short answer: triton kernels are great for dynamic shapes and can be lower latency on small seqs; cutlass/triton hybrid often best for long seqs. there's some noise by hardware generational differences. our plan: run both across your sample prompt set and pick the lower-P95 kernel family; we can also pin the runtime to prefer one family.
[05:05] Priya: quick note, Daniel earlier flagged occasional 500s in the logs, can you describe?
[05:12] Daniel: yeah when we stress-tested with seq_len 1024 and QPS burst to 120, we had timeouts from our side, unsure if it's backpressure or model OOMs.
[05:21] Liam: spikes to 120 QPS definitely can cause queueing. For dedicated we'd configure autoscaling + burst capacity; for hosted there's graceful fallback to a cheaper lower-capacity model for request shaping. We also have shedding policies to avoid OOMs.
[05:40] Evan: anything else on networking? our infra folks worry about cross region hops adding 10-20ms.
[05:47] Aisha: yep colocating in the same region is key, and for private deployment you'd host within your VPC to avoid egress. We'll share recommended region configs.
[05:58] Sofia: can you share the exact benchmark script you ran? we want to reproduce.
[06:02] Liam: already uploaded — link: https://redwood.app/benchmarks/rivermark/script.sh, includes config for batch sizes, seq_lens, streaming toggles. It's rough; apologies for inconsistent naming, the auto transcript might have mis-typed some values.
[06:20] Evan: on the note of mis-typing, in the doc one column says ttfm, i assume that's TTFT?
[06:26] Liam: yes ttfm is a bad shorthand, should be TTFT — will fix.
[06:30] Aisha: recap — liam will run deeper microbenchmarks focusing on kernel family and seq_len sweep. evan will send prod QPS and prompt set. aisha will send pricing and dedicated configs. any objections?
[06:44] Evan: sounds good. also can we include a security sync, we have a SOC2 audit next quarter.
[06:50] Priya: we have our security kit ready, will attach SOC2/ISO docs and a short answers doc, sending after meeting.
[06:59] Sofia: timeline — when can we expect the benchmark CSVs?
[07:02] Liam: aiming for 72 hours, so by 2027-04-02. I'll include TTFT, p50/p95/p99, CPU/GPU util, and kernel tag for each run.
[07:17] Daniel: great. for the follow-up deep dive on kernel selection, can we get someone from infra on that call? we may want to discuss custom kernel path.
[07:25] Liam: yes I'll loop in runtime infra. tentative weds 2027-04-06, i'll propose a time.
[07:33] Aisha: ok last bit — pricing, remember dedicated has reserved commit options, we can share three flavors (dev, prod, prod-plus) and sample SLA numbers.
[07:44] Evan: thanks.
[07:46] Aisha: any final questions?
[07:48] Sofia: one small one — does streaming require client-side changes?
[07:51] Liam: minimal; we expose the same API, streaming mode toggles chunk size. we also support websocket and http chunked.
[07:59] Evan: ok thanks everyone, look forward to the CSVs.
